meta.title: Who really said "Without courage, you can't practice any other virtue consistently"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Maya Angelou said it, and repeatedly. Verified in her Academy of Achievement interview; Wikiquote cites this popular wording to Stedman Graham's Diversity: Leaders Not Labels (2006).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Without courage, you can't practice any other virtue consistently'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Angelou — she said it on the record more than once. The exact wording drifts between tellings; here is the documented trail.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1928–2014 · American memoirist, poet and civil rights activist
answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and she said it more than once. The American Academy of Achievement’s published interview with Angelou carries the line almost exactly — “Because without courage, you cannot practice any other virtue consistently” ↗. Wikiquote cites the popular form — contraction, “erratically” sentence and all — to Stedman Graham’s Diversity: Leaders Not Labels (2006), p. 224, and the contraction wording to the Iconoclasts episode of 30 November 2006. Its USA Today citation of 5 March 1988 belongs to a different wording: “without courage we cannot practice any other virtue with consistency.”

source.excerpt: I suppose courage would be the first of his many wondrous and wonderful qualities that I would list. I am convinced that courage is the most important of all the virtues. Because without courage, you cannot practice any other virtue consistently.
trail: Quote Investigator has never had to take this one on: a site search for the saying ↗ returns nothing about it. Unlike the famous Angelou fakes, this line has not needed debunking.

Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries the exact popular wording — plus the second sentence that usually gets dropped — cited to Stedman Graham’s Diversity: Leaders Not Labels (2006), p. 224; a cognate wording, “without courage we cannot practice any other virtue with consistency,” is the one cited to her USA Today interview of 5 March 1988. The page also lists instances in the 1989 collection Conversations with Maya Angelou and the 2006 Iconoclasts episode with Dave Chappelle. The same page’s Misattributed section, which does list several Angelou fakes, leaves this line alone.

The American Academy of Achievement transcript ↗ has her saying it twice in one interview, both times about Martin Luther King Jr. — once describing him personally, once ranking the qualities that made him a leader.
A full-text search of scanned books ↗ returns dozens of printings, and where a credit appears it runs to Angelou — no rival claimant surfaces.

source.excerptNote: The transcript has it both ways: “you can’t practice any other virtues consistently” in one answer, “you cannot practice any other virtue consistently” in another — so even Angelou’s own phrasing shifted within one sitting.

author.name: Maya Angelou
author.heading: Who was Maya Angelou?
author.metaLine: 1928–2014 · American memoirist, poet and civil rights activist
author.bio: Born Marguerite Annie Johnson in St. Louis in 1928, Angelou turned a childhood of abuse and five years of silence into I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), the memoir that made her one of the most widely read authors in America. She served as northern coordinator for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and was a friend of both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X — which is why her remarks on courage tend to be about people she actually knew. In 1993 she read “On the Pulse of Morning” at Bill Clinton’s inauguration, the first poet to do so since Robert Frost in 1961.

misattribution.heading: The wording, not the author
misattribution.intro: For once, nobody else is trying to claim the line. The confusion here is about wording: Angelou made this point many times, each telling came out a little differently, and the version you meet online is a flattened composite of them.

items.why: The sourced text does not stop where the poster does. It runs on: “You can practice any virtue erratically, but nothing consistently without courage.” That second sentence is in Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ and almost never travels with the short form.

items.who: “we cannot practice any other virtue with consistency”
items.why: A longer version opening “One isn’t necessarily born with courage, but one is born with potential” has been reprinted in dozens of scanned books ↗. Same thought, different clothes — and it is this “with consistency” wording, not the popular contraction, that Wikiquote ↗ cites to USA Today of 5 March 1988.

Angelou used both numbers within a single Academy of Achievement interview ↗ — “any other virtues consistently” in one answer, “any other virtue consistently” in another. No single string can fairly be called the definitive text.

Angelou’s biography ↗ confirms she was giving interviews in this period, and Wikiquote attaches the “with consistency” wording — not the popular contraction — to the interview of 5 March 1988. No source pins the contraction form to 1988 at all; its earliest citations are from 2006. The article itself was not available to examine, so exactly what ran that day is left open here.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is sound — Angelou is on the record saying it ↗. Only the exact syllables are in question.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: She was not composing an aphorism; she was describing a friend. Asked which of Martin Luther King Jr.’s qualities made him a leader, Angelou put courage first, then explained why it outranks the warmer virtues: kindness, generosity and fairness are easy in short bursts, and it takes nerve to keep them up once they start costing you something.

That is the argument the poster version loses. Reduced to a single line, it reads like ordinary praise for bravery. In context it is a harder claim — that courage is not one virtue among many but the thing that makes all the others reliable.
context.detailsSummary: Why this page dates the source carefully
detailsBody: The Academy of Achievement publishes its Angelou interview under a High Point, North Carolina dateline of 22 January 1997, but the same page notes that the text was condensed from live broadcasts recorded in 1991, 1994 and 1997. The transcript is therefore solid evidence that Angelou said the line, while the particular sitting it came from is not pinned down — which is why nothing here claims she first said it on that date.

For the same reason this page does not assert an “earliest documented” use of its own. The earliest instance the specialists carry is a 1983 interview collected in Conversations with Maya Angelou (1989) — “Courage may be the most important of all the virtues because without it one cannot practice any other virtue with consistency” — and the next-earliest is the USA Today interview of 5 March 1988, again for the “with consistency” wording. Both citations are reported here as theirs.
